query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In steels used for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, the corrosion resistance is primarily governed by the rapid formation and sustained stability of a Cr-enriched passive oxide layer that is further stabilized by minor alloying elements such as Mo. This passivation layer minimizes ion transport and metal dissolution even under aggressive chemical and radiation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneous stainless steels with well-controlled compositions (e.g., >=18% Cr with minor Mo additions) produced via standard thermomechanical processing to yield a uniform microstructure and free of significant inclusions.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to controlled corrosive environments that mimic operating conditions (varying chloride ion concentrations, pH, elevated temperatures, and simulated radiation fields). Monitor the development and evolution of the passive film on the steel surfaces using electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) and surface analysis techniques (X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning/transmission electron microscopy).
generation.conditions: Tests will be conducted in aqueous solutions with different chloride concentrations (e.g., 0.1 M, 1.0 M, and 3.5% NaCl) and at temperatures ranging from ambient to approximately 120°C. Samples will be simultaneously subjected to controlled radiation doses representative of nuclear-power operational conditions compared to analogous non-irradiated controls. The baseline is defined by steel samples tested in low-chloride, room-temperature, non-irradiated environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, nanocrystalline Cr2O3-rich passive film that forms within minutes of exposure and is stabilized by the presence of alloying modifiers like Mo, which help suppress localized breakdowns (pitting) in the oxide film.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to the aggressive aqueous environment, Cr from the steel surface rapidly oxidizes to form a dense Cr2O3 layer. This film decreases ionic and electronic transport, thus mitigating further oxidation and metal dissolution. Minor additions, such as Mo, enhance the film's integrity and facilitate self-healing in the event of mechanical or radiolytic damage. Under radiation, although defect generation in the passive film is possible, its composition and close adherence to the substrate help maintain its barrier properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to baseline conditions, steels exposed to higher chloride concentrations and simulated radiation will form thicker, more enriched Cr2O3 passive films that exhibit lower corrosion current densities and higher impedance values. Improved film stability with less evidence of pitting or localized breakdown should correlate with increased alloying levels of Cr (and Mo), while steels with lower Cr content or lacking Mo will show faster breakdown of passivity and higher corrosion rates.
generation.baseline: Conventional low-alloy steels or stainless steels with lower Cr content, which under identical test conditions develop less uniform or thinner passive films and display higher measured corrosion rates and pitting incidence.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to aqueous environments typical in chemical-processing plants and light-water nuclear reactors (up to around 120°C) and under moderate radiation fluxes. Its applicability may be limited in extremely high-temperature (>300°C) or supercritical conditions where film behavior alters significantly, or in steels with heterogeneous microstructures or significant inclusion content.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise impact of radiation on the defect chemistry and long-term evolution of the passive film, as well as the kinetics of film repair in high chloride environments. The synergistic effects of radiation and aggressive chemistry on film morphology warrant further experimental delineation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative study wherein high-Cr/Mo steels and lower-Cr steels are exposed simultaneously to identical aggressive environments (varying chloride concentrations, elevated temperatures, and simulated radiation). Use surface analytical techniques (XPS, TEM) to quantify the chemical composition, thickness, and continuity of the passive film. Electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization and EIS) will be used to monitor corrosion rates and film stability over time. Compare the responses of the high-Cr/Mo steels to the baseline low-Cr steels.
measurements: XPS analysis of surface oxide composition (quantification of Cr2O3 content)
TEM measurement of passive film thickness and microstructure
Potentiodynamic polarization to determine corrosion current densities
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess barrier properties
Optical/SEM imaging for pit initiation and growth
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-Cr/Mo steels do not exhibit a significantly thicker, more continuous, and chemically enriched passive film with correspondingly lower corrosion current densities compared to the baseline low-Cr steels under identical aggressive conditions, then the mechanistic hypothesis is rejected.
